demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I feel isolated and set apart from others
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Physical pain in the same body parts as during the event is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, unless the patient was also physically injured during the event. That makes this item clinically implausible from the provided trauma context.

A global mistrust appraisal is a weak fit with bereavement trauma unless there is some interpersonal betrayal, negligence, or assault-related context. The rest of the profile centers on loss, alarm, and isolation rather than interpersonal threat from other people, so this item is not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, ambulances can plausibly cue the death context and workplace cues may be idiosyncratically linked, but 'People cycling' is hard to connect clinically unless the loved one died in a cycling-related incident, which is not reflected anywhere else in threat, appraisals, or memory. It stands out as a trigger with no supporting context in the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by grief-related recall and affective reliving without clear imagery, which fits bereavement trauma. 'Intense shame' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the negative appraisals, which focus on identity loss, isolation, and life destruction rather than self-blame, guilt, or humiliation. In this profile, shame is insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and trauma type.

vignette: On a wet Tuesday afternoon in late spring, Kwame was driving his battered blue pickup from the paint shop back toward the neighborhood where his wife, Aisha, had just finished her shift at the local nursing home. He had barely passed the corner when an elderly gentleman fell across the center lane, a sudden impact that sent the car into a skid. The crash was swift and unforgiving; a siren wailed in the distance and, within seconds, a line of bright red emergency lights flashed by. Ambulances rattled past, the doors swinging open and closed as paramedics worked on the victim. Kwame's hands tightened around the wheel, his heart pounding. He felt an unearthly shock that would ripple through his life for years to come. The same images of flashing lights and frantic voices kept resurfacing when he walked into the paint shop on subsequent days, or when he tried to recount the day to a friend over coffee. The mere sight of an ambulance signaled a looming threat; Kwame's body went into a state of constant alert, his muscles tensing as if he were in the middle of a battle. Nightfall brought a different kind of dread: he could not find peace even inside his own home, feeling as though a phantom danger lurked behind every dark corner. When he tried to close his eyes, memories burst back as vivid, disjointed pictures of the accident, and he found himself crying for the loss of the man who had died that afternoon. These images, though they lacked a clear narrative, carried the same fierce grief he felt the next day, the grief that made him believe his life had been shattered. The constant vigilance and the memory flashes began to reinforce one another, each intensifying the other. The repeated exposure to scenes of emergency contexts, the stress of being in a workplace that was now associated with the trauma, and the constant talk among colleagues about loved ones lost, all served to amplify this loop. Whenever someone mentioned a tragedy, Kwame's mind would race back to the ambulance and the suddenness of death, and the memory would flood him with emotional intensity, a sense of grief that felt almost as real as the event itself. He began to think that his identity was no longer his own; that he had lost something essential and could not find his way back. That sense of identity loss, that feeling of isolation, and the belief that his life had been destroyed by a single moment, fed into his fear. These negative appraisals made him feel even more threatened, because he saw the world as a place where anything could end him or his wife in an instant. The belief that he was unmoored and powerless only pushed him further into the cycle: each time the memory of the accident surfaced, it drove him to feel unsafe, and each sense of threat, in turn, made the memory more vivid and the negative appraisal more potent. The triggers, the memory, the threat, and the negative appraisals fed each other in a tightening loop that became a constant presence in his life. Over the next few months, the nightly vigilance turned into a habit. Kwame would lock every door, turn on every light, and never let himself fall into a slump that might make him feel exposed. Even while he slept, his body stayed on edge, as if it were poised to spring into action at a single alarm. He would frequently pause mid-walk to glance behind him, convinced that danger lurked in plain sight. When he remembered the day of the crash, the images of the ambulance and the sharp, metallic sound of the siren would come flooding back, and he would feel an acute, all-encompassing grief that seemed to swallow his thoughts. He would spend hours on the phone with his wife, his voice trembling as he described how his body felt constantly tense, how the night seemed far more perilous than daylight. The loss of his sense of self was a quiet, daily ache that gnawed at him whenever he tried to focus on his work or on their shared future. At the paint shop, Kwame found that the work environment itself had become a source of distress. The sound of the shop's overhead fan, the sight of the freshly sprayed walls, even the faint hum of the refrigeration unit-all of these could trigger an involuntary surge of panic, as if the machinery itself could be a harbinger of danger. He started arriving early and leaving early, refusing to stay for the long after-hours shift that his colleagues often took to finish up projects. The social aspect of the workplace was also compromised; when coworkers spoke about their own losses or brought up stories of recent funerals, Kwame would become reticent, his mind spiraling back to the ambulance and the sudden loss of his wife's life. The cumulative effect of these experiences had eroded the fabric of his daily life. He no longer felt a sense of belonging at work, and his relationship with Aisha grew strained as he withdrew from shared activities. The constant threat of an emergency, the recurring vivid memories, the relentless grief, and the feeling that he had lost his identity-all of these compounded into a profound sense of isolation. The day he finally sat across from the therapist, Kwame's voice cracked as he admitted that he was terrified of another sudden death, terrified that he could never feel safe again, and terrified that his life would forever be a series of anxious anticipations. He clung to the hope that he could learn to trust again, that the relentless vigilance could be replaced by a calm presence, and that he might one day reclaim the sense of self he feared had been lost.
